extraction.name: Common Corpus: The Largest Collection of Ethical Data for LLM Pre-Training
extraction.description: Common Corpus is a large open multilingual dataset for language model pre-training, assembled from public domain and permissively licensed sources across government, culture, science, code, web, and semantic data. The paper describes provenance, filtering, curation, OCR correction, PII removal, and toxicity filtering, and reports about 2 trillion tokens.
extraction.creator: Pierre-Carl Langlais, Carlos Rosas Hinostroza, Mattia Nee, Catherine Amett, Pavel Chizhov, Eliot Krzystof Jones, Irène Girard, David Mach, Anastasia Stasenko, Ivan P. Yamshchikov
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The corpus was assembled from multiple sources and collections, including public domain and permissively licensed documents. The paper states that Open Culture was compiled from Collections As Data initiatives and resource-by-resource retrieval using APIs and other standard retrieval methods; Open Science was collected via OpenAlex and direct arXiv extraction; Open Code came from The Stack v1 and v2; Open Web included Wikipedia/Wikisource, YouTube Commons, and StackExchange; Open Semantic included Wikidata adapted into natural language. The dataset was curated and filtered, with provenance and license information recorded for most documents.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Web API, Document analysis, Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper explicitly notes missing or incomplete metadata for many web sources, stating that most web data do not have sufficient metadata to determine permissive licensing. It also mentions poor OCR quality, text segmentation issues, and irrecoverable deterioration of original support for some cultural heritage documents.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Public domain and permissively licensed documents from government, cultural heritage, scientific, code, web, and semantic sources, including SEC filings, WTO documents, AMF documents, TED EU tenders, GATT Library, Europarl, Caselaw Access Project, CourtListener, EUR-lex, Eurovoc, French open data, USPTO, UN Digital Library, OECD, Chronicle America, Europeana, Gallica, Biblioteca, Library of Congress books and newspapers, Delpher, Wikimedia projects, YouTube Commons, StackExchange, OpenAlex, arXiv, The Stack v1/v2, and Wikidata.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The effort began in 2024; the paper states the current version was released in February 2025 and that some included sources span historical periods from 1658 to 2024 depending on the subcollection.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The paper describes several transformations: OCR correction using OCRonos, OCR quality detection using OCRoscope and OCRerrcr, text segmentation using Segmentext, PII replacement with fictitious but realistic values using Microsoft Presidio and custom regex patterns, toxicity filtering and synthetic rewriting of harmful public-domain text using Celadon, removal of files outside desired languages/formats, filtering of non-permissible licenses, removal of files with 75% or more digits, and recalculation of line lengths after replacing carriage-return/newline sequences.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Data were filtered by language and file format, non-permissible licenses were removed, low-quality code files were filtered using manual filters, files with mostly digits were removed, OCR errors were detected and corrected, PII was replaced, and harmful content was removed or rewritten before the data were made suitable for pre-training.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The paper does not describe a human annotation protocol for the dataset itself. It does state that Celadon, a toxicity classifier used in curation, was trained from scratch on 2M annotated samples, but the annotation creation process for those samples is not described here. EUR-lex documents were annotated by the Publications Office of the EU with concepts from EuroVoc.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: No explicit analysis of annotation disagreement, uncertainty, or label aggregation is described for Common Corpus. The paper only notes that Celadon was trained on 2M annotated samples and that EUR-lex documents were annotated with EuroVoc concepts.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Segmentext, OCRoscope, OCRerrcr, OCRonos, Microsoft Presidio, Celadon
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The paper states that Common Corpus is an evolving resource rather than a fixed dataset, with HuggingFace ensuring archiving of past versions for reproducibility. It also says the current version was released in February 2025 and that future releases will continue to expand the corpus.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Personally identifiable information (PII) such as phone numbers, email addresses, and IP addresses is explicitly discussed as being removed or replaced. The paper also mentions sensitive/harmful content dimensions including race and origin-based bias, gender and sexuality-based bias, religious bias, ability bias, and violence and abuse.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper frames the dataset as supporting open science and legally compliant LLM pre-training, reducing dependence on restricted web data and enabling reproducible models. It also discusses broader societal concerns around copyright, AI legislation, access to knowledge, and harmful content reproduction, and positions the corpus as open AI infrastructure serving the public interest.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper notes that web data can contain sexual content, hate speech, and racial and gender biases, and that historical public-domain texts may reflect outdated cultural norms about ethnic groups, women, and violence. It also states that toxicity filtering was used to mitigate some of these biases.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Common Corpus does not cover the entire range of available open data, has shallow coverage for low-resource languages, is not directly suitable for instruction-tuning or specialized task fine-tuning, and larger models may require more data than the corpus currently provides. The paper also notes that curation methods are not perfectly accurate and that OCR errors remain challenging.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for pre-training large language models and can be used on its own or with existing open datasets. The paper also mentions use for multilingual language models, creative writing models, historical language models, vision-language models for document segmentation and processing, retrieval-augmented models, classifiers, synthetic datasets, benchmarks, and ethical fine-tuning dataset creation.
